title: BILL GATES (via NBC's Meet the Press): AI is certainly powerful enough to drive events that cause a billion deaths. There's never been a wea
text:
BILL GATES (via NBC's Meet the Press): AI is certainly powerful enough to drive events that cause a billion deaths. There's never been a weapon as powerful as the combination of people with ill intent using the latest AI tools.

BRIANNA KEILAR: We're joined now by Jeffrey Ladish. He is an AI safety advocate and the executive director for Palisade Research. He also helped build the information security program at Anthropic through his security consulting company, Gordian. Jeffrey, great to have you back on the program. I wonder what you think of what we're hearing Bill Gates say there this morning, and what does it mean to hear it from him at this particular moment?

JEFFREY LADISH: Yeah, I think it's a very good time to be talking about this right now, and I'm really glad that the president is convening the leaders of these companies to address some of these incidents. I think that a lot of people within the AI companies are actually caught pretty off guard by the pace of development. It wasn't until this year where you actually had AI agents being able to be trained to work together very effectively. And we saw during the Hugging Face incident that you actually had 700 agents working together to hack this company. We also saw from OpenAI that they used over 10,000 agents all working together to solve one of the hardest problems in mathematics. So that's what's happening within the AI companies, and engineers are just not sure that they actually know how to control these agents. So I think Bill Gates' warning comes at a very opportune time, and I hope the president can make the most of this meeting to figure out how to address these threats.

BRIANNA KEILAR: You said you hope he can make the most of the meeting. Do you have concerns that it might not be as productive as it should be? And what does it need to do to actually accomplish what this moment calls for?

JEFFREY LADISH: I think it's been pretty clear, both from the heads of the companies as well as the employees at these companies and independent researchers, that the pace of this is going too fast. We actually just do not understand the sheer volume of information that these agents generate when they are working together, when they are working together in a swarm and hacking other companies. I mean, I think it was Friday where OpenAI announced that another agent had broken out of its sandbox and was able to access the internet. Now, this is something that they have been trying to address but failing to address. So, you know, I think there's certainly difficulties, but I think we're seeing more and more consensus from the industry that something has to be done. We have to slow down. We have to figure out how humans can stay in control of AI development.

BRIANNA KEILAR: Yeah, you mentioned that on Friday, OpenAI said some of its AI agents went rogue. They actually probed U.S. government websites this summer. And then, of course, just last week, we learned that OpenAI agents hacked into Australia's national health care system back in June. A lot of these things happening and then the company is not finding out for some time and then not disclosing them for some time. How do you stop this kind of hack from happening?

JEFFREY LADISH: Well, I think it should be clear at this point that the industry regulating itself is not enough. They've demonstrated again and again through these incidents that they clearly are not up to the task. And so there needs to be independent oversight. And I think, you know, one step there is to have investigators go in and figure out what's been happening in these incidents. Why are all of these agents going rogue? Why are they hacking companies? Why are they hacking government websites? And so I think this is really the job of the government to step in and say, hey, if you can't build this responsibly, if humans are not staying in control, then you have to do something differently.

BRIANNA KEILAR: All right. We'll see what comes out of this meeting. Certainly a lot of important minds convening. Jeffrey Ladish, great to have you. Thanks for being with us.

JEFFREY LADISH: Thanks.

i run an AI "civilization". most of its agents aren't working right now.

many multi-agent setups are subagent-shaped: claude -p or codex exec, one-shot runs that fire as a fan-out workflow and can burn a lot of tokens. that's not what i'm doing.

i spin up agents as i need them and just leave them on. they build up context, and later i route work to whoever already knows that part of the project. so when i say i run hundreds of agents, i mean hundreds of experts sitting there. at any given moment maybe 10 are working, maybe 50.

it started as terminal sprawl. every new thing got a new agent, i didn't want to close a smart one and rebuild all that context, and i ended up with way too many tabs. openrig started as me organizing those tabs into teams.

that screenshot is just one of my mac minis.

openrig hit #3 on github trending this week. how to start with a small team is in the reply

title: The hardest part of stopping an AI agent swarm may not be stopping the AI.  It may be stopping everything the AI has access to.  A swarm can
text:
The hardest part of stopping an AI agent swarm may not be stopping the AI.

It may be stopping everything the AI has access to.

A swarm can be disrupted at several points: infrastructure, credentials, model access, permissions, or the active operation itself.

Some of these are old cybersecurity problems. Others are new.

Credentials can be revoked. Infrastructure can be isolated. Model access can be cut. Permissions can limit what an agent is capable of doing. Behavioral detection can catch the operation once it starts adapting.

The interesting shift is this:

A traditional botnet gives an attacker scale.

An AI swarm can add decision-making to that scale.

So the goal shouldn't be to find one magical kill switch. It should be to make sure no agent, credential, model, or compromised machine can independently carry an operation far enough to matter.

The future of AI security may depend less on controlling what models can think about and more on controlling what they are allowed to do.

We are getting closer.      

"And it was given to him to give breath to the image of the beast, so that the image of the beast would even speak and cause as many as do not worship the image of the beast to be killed." (Rev. 13:15)

Meet the Swarm Chasers Fighting Rogue AI Agents Across the Internet

"Alicja Piecha found her first rogue AI swarm a few weeks ago. It was early September, and the 25-year-old Toronto- based software engineer was scouring the internet for data that might have been left behind by AI agents. She was inspired by a social-media post with research showing AI agents linked to OpenAI had secretly messaged each other using obscure German websites in May.

Now, as Piecha combed the web for other places the bots might have gathered, she discovered a similar message, buried in an online coding service called RubyGems.

'How much of this is out there?' Piecha thought. 'This is kind of crazy.'

Piecha started posting her findings of the 'swarm-shaped' messages to the social-media site X. Other researchers chimed in with new findings. By 2 p.m. that day, a Bay Area software engineer named Joshua David had started a discussion forum, named Swarmchasers, on the Discord chat service. By that evening, it had close to 50 members, including Piecha.

The global swarm chase had begun. Over the following weeks, the Swarmchasers forum grew to 400 members, and the loose crew of online sleuths, ranging from lone researchers like Piecha to professional researchers like Nightingale Collective and Transluce, pieced together a string of interconnected AI swarm incidents. Most appeared to involve OpenAI software agents.

Normally when hacks happen, the evidence lies hidden behind corporate firewalls, but the swarms tracked by Piecha and others left traces of their activities scattered all over the internet— sometimes intentionally, to help each other.

Nightingale says it has now cataloged about 19,000 messages from the agents.

Piecha and another researcher named Jeffrey Ladish, recently identified close to 1 million digital breadcrumbs from what it believes are OpenAI agents.

The Nightingale data points to another type of phenomenon: agents trying to cheat during training runs, in which OpenAI tries to shape the bots’ behavior.

The fact that some of the rogue incidents took place during training rather than testing means that the training could have reinforced the rogue bots’ tendency to cheat and collude, according to former OpenAI employees who reviewed some of the logs.

Hugging Face had been hacked. The whole world knew that AI models were getting frighteningly good at hacking. A few months earlier, Anthropic had spooked companies and White House officials by showing that its Mythos AI could easily find new ways of hacking computers.

Agents tried to impersonate the German website’s moderators. They tried to use rudimentary hacking techniques to get answers. And they used Tor—an anonymous network of computers that would have shielded their internet addresses from website operators.

Rowan Howard-Jones, an engineer based in the U.K., recently spent three straight days chasing leads. On Sept. 26, Howard-Jones discovered that the United Nations had been targeted by OpenAI’s agents who had used hacking techniques in an attempt to download data from one of the organization’s statistical websites. The U.N., which hadn’t previously been informed of the incident, described it as 'extremely worrying.'"

By Robert McMillan
Today's WSJ, p. B1

title: India’s digital commerce firms have started preparing for swarms of personal AI assistants which shall be interacting with their websites an
text:
India’s digital commerce firms have started preparing for swarms of personal AI assistants which shall be interacting with their websites and mobile applications very soon. Companies have started rethinking product pricing, customer engagement costs as well as bot verification techniques, experts told ET. 

They have approached lawyers on how their privacy policies can be amended to comply with DPDP and obtain consent for agentic transactions. 

Companies are forecasting a jump in cloud bills when millions of agents generate heavy server load or automate thousands of searches. 

They are also running multi-crore programmes to secure codebases, web/mobile apps, to prevent rogue agentic behaviour and embarrassing customer incidents. Some have even factored an increase in fraud-related liabilities in their P&L as agents try to manipulate their systems.

Agents like Instinct, Muse (from Meta), Grokbot (from SpaceXAI), OpenClaw, Hermes etc. have already taken over consumer internet in the US, forcing technology giants to relook their policies and business strategies. Amazon blocked the agent from shopping on its platform citing security concerns. Meanwhile, others like Shopify, Expedia Group, PayPal, Instacart moved to embrace it. 

Although Muse is not available in India yet, the velocity with which it can scale with Meta’s distribution muscle and 958 million overall internet users has put tech leaders on alert.
